To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the regulation of the IgA production in the serum and in parodid saliva are different in HIV infected patients and that the IgA/IgA antibody ratio in parodid is lower in HIV infected subjects than in controls.
HIV‐1 infection is associated with an imbalance of IgA and secreted IgA (s‐IgA) in saliva and that the regulation of these antibodies is independent in serum, and in parotids.

the regulation of immunoglobulin production in serum and parotid salivary glands of HIV‐1‐positive patients is different and that this imbalance of IgA and HIV‐1‐specific antibodies may be important in terms of local mucosal protection after immunization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods of diagnosis and treatment of AIDS.
the study of the immunological status of HIV‐1 infected patients, with special reference to the humoral response to HIV‐1 antigens.
the study of the immune response in HIV‐1‐ infected subjects and the development of a diagnostic tool based on the measurement of IgA antibodies to viral proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mucosal immune system in HIV‐1 infection is not only altered but is probably also a target for the virus.
the mucosal immune system in the oral cavity is not impaired by the HIV‐infection.

the mucosal immune system in HIV‐1 infected individuals is not able to respond appropriately to HIV‐1 antigens, and that this may be one of the factors responsible for the high susceptibility to mucosal infections in this group of patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IgA/IgA ratio is significantly lower in saliva than in serum of HIV‐1‐positive individuals.
HIV‐1 infection is characterized by an increase of serum IgG, IgM and IgA concentrations, but not of IgA in parotid secretion.
the IgA response in the saliva of HIV‐1 infected patients was not as strong and specific as that of the serum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regulation of immunoglobulines in serum and saliva in HIV‐1 infected patients is independent.

the mucosal immune response to HIV‐1 is different in serum and in the parotid saliva of HIV‐infected patients and that the regulation of the IgA and IgA production at mucosal level seems independent of that of serum.
the regulation of immunoglobulin production is independent in serum, saliva, and mucosal secretions.
